question: Under the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, on what grounds is discrimination against citizens prohibited in law or in public appointments, except as the Constitution expressly authorises?
answer: There shall be no discrimination against citizens on the ground only of religion, race, descent or place of birth in any law or in appointment to office or employment under a public authority.
gold_citations: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Art 12(2)
evidence_quote: there shall be no discrimination against citizens of Singapore on the ground only of religion, race, descent or place of birth in any law or in the appointment to any office or employment under a public authority

question: Under the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, which freedoms are guaranteed to citizens by Article 14(1)?
answer: Subject to restrictions Parliament may impose by law, every citizen has the right to freedom of speech and expression, the right to assemble peaceably and without arms, and the right to form associations.
gold_citations: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Art 14(1)
evidence_quote: every citizen of Singapore has the right to freedom of speech and expression; (b) all citizens of Singapore have the right to assemble peaceably and without arms; and (c) all citizens of Singapore have the right to form associations.

question: Under the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, what is the maximum number of non-constituency Members of Parliament?
answer: Parliament may include non-constituency Members not exceeding 12 in number, as provided by law relating to Parliamentary elections.
gold_citations: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Art 39(1)(b)
evidence_quote: such other Members, not exceeding 12 in number, who shall be known as non-constituency Members

question: I signed a contract with an arbitration clause, but the other side sued me in court instead. Can I get the court case put on hold?
answer: Yes. A party to the arbitration agreement may apply to the court to stay the proceedings, at any time after filing and serving a notice of intention to contest or not contest and before delivering any pleading or taking any other step.
evidence_quote: may, at any time after filing and serving a notice of intention to contest or not contest and before delivering any pleading

question: Under the International Arbitration Act 1994, when may a party apply to stay court proceedings brought in breach of an international arbitration agreement?
answer: Despite Article 8 of the Model Law, a party may apply at any time after filing and serving a notice of intention to contest or not contest and before delivering any pleading or taking any other step in the proceedings.
evidence_quote: Despite Article 8 of the Model Law, where any party to an arbitration agreement to which this Act applies institutes any proceedings in any court against any other party to the agreement

question: Under the Apostille Act 2020, to what documents does the Part on producing foreign public documents apply?
answer: It applies to a foreign public document sought to be produced in Singapore for any purpose, including court or tribunal proceedings and exercising powers or performing duties under written law.
evidence_quote: This Part applies to a foreign public document sought to be produced in Singapore for any purpose, including — (a) the purposes of proceedings in any court or tribunal; and

question: I'm a permanent resident who can't afford a lawyer for a civil case. Am I eligible for legal aid?
answer: Legal aid may be given to a citizen or permanent resident of Singapore for civil proceedings listed in Part 1 of the Schedule to the Legal Aid and Advice Act 1995, excluding those in Part 2, subject to the Act's conditions.
gold_citations: Legal Aid and Advice Act 1995, s 5(1)
evidence_quote: legal aid may be given to a citizen or permanent resident of Singapore in relation to any civil proceedings mentioned in Part 1 of the Schedule

question: Under the Online Criminal Harms Act 2023, when may a designated officer give a Part 2 direction in respect of online activity?
answer: When the officer reasonably suspects a specified offence has been committed and online activity furthers it, or suspects or has reason to believe the online activity is preparatory to or in furtherance of a scam or malicious cyber activity.
evidence_quote: reasonably suspects that a specified offence has been committed and that any online activity is in furtherance of the commission of the offence; or

question: My elderly father is convinced by scammers and keeps trying to send them money. Can the authorities stop his bank from letting him transfer money?
answer: Yes. A specified officer may issue a restriction order directing banks not to allow transfers or withdrawals from the scam victim's accounts, or credit facilities, if there is reason to believe the victim will transfer money to a scammer.
evidence_quote: allow a transfer or withdrawal of money from any bank account of the scam victim maintained with that bank;

question: Under the Protection from Scams Act 2025, what may a restriction order direct banks not to do?
answer: It directs the bank not to allow a transfer or withdrawal of money from the scam victim's accounts and not to grant, or allow a drawdown of, any credit facility to the scam victim while the order is in force.
evidence_quote: (ii) grant, or allow a drawdown of, any credit facility to the scam victim;

question: Under the Public Defenders Act 2022, what must the Chief Public Defender consider when agreeing fees with a panel solicitor?
answer: The Chief Public Defender must have regard to whether the fees are reasonable and proportionate, taking into account relevant factors.
evidence_quote: the Chief Public Defender must have regard to whether the fees are reasonable and proportionate

question: Under the Extradition Act 1968, what is the liability of a fugitive from a foreign State to which the relevant Part applies?
answer: Every fugitive from that State or territory is liable to be apprehended and surrendered to it, subject to that Part and any limitations, conditions, exceptions or qualifications on its application to that State or territory.
evidence_quote: every fugitive from that State or territory is liable to be apprehended and surrendered to that State or territory, subject to — (a) this Part;

question: Under the Internal Security Act 1960, for what maximum period may a detention order direct that a person be detained?
answer: The Minister may make an order directing that the person be detained for any period not exceeding 2 years, where the President is satisfied this is necessary to prevent the person acting prejudicially to Singapore's security, public order or essential services.
evidence_quote: (a) directing that such person be detained for any period not exceeding 2 years; or

question: Under the Police Force Act 2004, what are the functions of the Police Force throughout Singapore?
answer: Its functions are to maintain law and order, preserve public peace, prevent and detect crimes, apprehend offenders, and exercise any other function conferred by written law.
evidence_quote: (a) to maintain law and order; (b) to preserve public peace; (c) to prevent and detect crimes; (d) to apprehend offenders;

question: Under the Application of English Law Act 1993, to what extent does the common law of England continue to be part of Singapore law?
answer: The common law of England, including equity, continues to be part of Singapore law so far as it was part of that law immediately before 12 November 1993, and so far as it is applicable to Singapore's circumstances, subject to modifications those circumstances require.
gold_citations: Application of English Law Act 1993, s 3(1)–(2)
evidence_quote: so far as it was part of the law of Singapore immediately before 12 November 1993, continues to be part of the law of Singapore.

question: Under the Choice of Court Agreements Act 2016, what must a Singapore court do with a case covered by an exclusive choice of court agreement that designates no Singapore court?
answer: The Singapore court must stay or dismiss the case unless it determines that one of the listed exceptions applies, such as the agreement being null and void under the law of the State of the chosen court.
gold_citations: Choice of Court Agreements Act 2016, s 12(1)
evidence_quote: a Singapore court must stay or dismiss any case or proceeding to which the agreement applies, unless the Singapore court determines that — (a) the agreement is null and void under the law of the State of the chosen court;

question: Under the Intoxicating Substances Act 1987, what conduct constitutes the offence of misuse of intoxicating substances?
answer: A person commits an offence if, for the purpose of inducing or causing in themselves a state of intoxication, they use or inhale any intoxicating substance.
evidence_quote: A person must not, for the purpose of inducing or causing in himself or herself a state of intoxication, use or inhale any intoxicating substance.

question: Under the Arms Offences Act 1973, if a person fires a gun at someone and claims they had no intention to injure, what intention is presumed and what punishment follows on conviction?
answer: The person is presumed, until the contrary is proved, to have used the gun intending to injure or endanger another person's safety, and using or attempting to use a gun with such intent is punishable with death.
evidence_quote: shall, until the contrary is proved, be presumed to have used or attempted to use the gun intending to injure, or endanger the safety of, another person

question: Under the Civil Law Act 1909, if an unmarried person with no children is killed by another's wrongful act, who can benefit from a claim for bereavement damages?
answer: A wrongful death action may include a bereavement claim; where there is no surviving spouse or children, the claim is for the benefit of the deceased's parents, or the mother if the deceased was illegitimate.
evidence_quote: the parents of the deceased or, if the deceased was illegitimate, his mother;

question: Under the Interpretation Act 1965, if a written law requires something to be done within 6 days of an event that happened on a Monday, and none of the days is a public holiday, what is the last day for doing it?
answer: The day of the event is excluded, so the 6-day period runs Tuesday to Sunday; because the last day is a Sunday, the period extends to the next day that is not excluded, making the deadline the following Monday.
evidence_quote: a period of days from the happening of an event or the doing of any act or thing is deemed to be exclusive of the day on which the event happens or the act or thing is done;

question: Under the Limitation Act 1959, if a contract claim is based on the defendant's fraud that the claimant only discovered 4 years after the cause of action accrued, when does the 6-year limitation period expire?
answer: Contract actions are barred 6 years after the cause of action accrues, but for actions based on fraud the period does not begin to run until the fraud is discovered or could reasonably have been discovered, so it expires 6 years from that discovery date.
evidence_quote: (a) the action is based upon the fraud of the defendant or his agent or of any person through whom he claims or his agent;

question: Under the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act 2014, how do the maximum fine and imprisonment for a second trafficking offence compare with a first offence?
answer: A first offence carries a fine up to $100,000 and imprisonment up to 10 years, while a second or subsequent offence carries a fine up to $150,000, imprisonment up to 15 years and caning up to 9 strokes.
gold_citations: Prevention of Human Trafficking Act 2014, s 4(1)(a)–(b)
evidence_quote: in the case of a second or subsequent offence, shall be punished with a fine not exceeding $150,000, with imprisonment for a term not exceeding 15 years

question: Under the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act 1955, what consent does the Minister need to order detention of a person associated with criminal activities, and for how long may the order run?
answer: The Minister needs the consent of the Public Prosecutor, and a detention order may direct detention for any period not exceeding 12 months from the date of the order.
evidence_quote: the Minister may, with the consent of the Public Prosecutor — (a) if he is satisfied that it is necessary that the person be detained in the interests of public safety, peace and good order

question: Under the Penal Code 1871, what are the elements of theft and what is its maximum term of imprisonment?
answer: Theft is committed by moving movable property out of another's possession without consent, intending to take it dishonestly; it is punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both.
evidence_quote: Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person’s consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft.

question: In Chew Kim Kee v Kertar and Co [2004] SGHC 95, by what date did a notice of appeal against the district judge's Order have to be filed, and was it filed?
answer: Under the Rules of Court a notice of appeal had to be filed within 14 days of the Order, by 5 October 1999, and it was not disputed that the defendant did not file one by that date or at all.
evidence_quote: Under the Rules of Court, a notice of appeal must be filed within 14 days of the order — in this case, by 5 October 1999.

question: When a lawyer misses a court filing deadline, what test do courts use to decide whether the lawyer breached their duty of care?
answer: A breach occurs if, on the balance of probabilities, the lawyer omitted to do something a reasonably competent advocate and solicitor in their position would have done, which includes observing the Rules of Court.
evidence_quote: omitted to do a thing which a reasonably competent advocate and solicitor in their position would have done

question: If I fire my lawyer but the firm is still listed as my solicitor on the court record, does that mean their retainer continues?
answer: No. In a solicitor's negligence claim, the court rejected the argument that the retainer had not been terminated merely because there was no order to discharge the firm as solicitor on record, finding no merit in that submission.
evidence_quote: a reason which Mr Loo cited for saying the retainer had not been terminated was that there was no order to discharge the firm as solicitor on record. There is no merit in his submission.

question: In Chew Kim Kee v Kertar and Co [2004] SGHC 95, what did the plaintiff do with the matrimonial home after the Order, and what was the outcome of her action?
answer: She exercised the option to buy over the other 65% share of the matrimonial home and resold it in March 2001 for $1.4m at a small profit; her action against the solicitors was dismissed with costs.
evidence_quote: It transpired that she exercised the option and bought over the other 65% share of the matrimonial home. She subsequently resold the property in March 2001 for $1.4m

question: In Amutha Valli d/o Krishnan v Titular Superior of the Redemptorist Fathers in Singapore [2009] SGHC 35, did the court find that the defendants' actions at the Church caused the plaintiff damage?
answer: No. The court found she had not suffered PTSD and that the defendants' actions on 10 August 2004 did not cause her any damage, so her claim on all three causes of action was dismissed.
evidence_quote: I therefore find that the actions of the defendants at the Church on the night of 10 August 2004 did not cause the plaintiff to suffer any damage.

question: In Tan & Au LLP v Goh Teh Lee [2012] SGHC 130, what judgment sum was awarded to the law firm and what happened to the client's counterclaim?
answer: Judgment was given for the plaintiff firm for $23,703.66, inclusive of interest charged by Merrill Legal Solutions, with costs, and the defendant's counterclaim was dismissed with costs.
evidence_quote: judgment is given to the plaintiff for the sum of $23,703.66 (inclusive of the interest charged by Merrill Legal Solutions as claimed in the statement of claim) and costs. The defendant's counterclaim is dismissed with costs.

question: In Chan Susan v Lai Tet Chong [2012] SGHC 139, was the first defendant found to have breached a duty of care to the plaintiff?
answer: No. The court agreed the first defendant was not in breach of any duty of care in the circumstances, held the plaintiff had failed to prove her case, and dismissed the claim.
evidence_quote: I agree with Mr Wee that the first defendant was not in breach of any duty of care to the plaintiff in these circumstances.

question: In Anwar Patrick Adrian v Ng Chong & Hue LLC [2013] SGHC 202, were the solicitor Ng and his firm held liable for the plaintiffs' loss?
answer: No. Although Ng was not careful about whom he acted for and did not spot the personal liability clauses in the mortgage documents, the court held he and NC&H were not liable and dismissed the action with costs.
evidence_quote: I am of the view that he and NC&H are not liable for the loss claimed by the first and second plaintiffs in this action.

question: If a lawyer bungles the signing of a will so it isn't valid, can the people who were meant to inherit recover their losses from the lawyer?
answer: Yes, in the right circumstances. In one case the intended beneficiaries made out their negligence claim against the solicitors and were held entitled to their claimed loss of AUD$719,375.36 and 50m rupiah.
evidence_quote: I am satisfied that the plaintiffs have made out their claim in negligence against the defendants and are, accordingly, entitled to their total claimed loss of AUD$719,375.36 and 50m rupiah.

question: In AEL v Cheo Yeoh & Associates LLC [2014] SGHC 129, why were the plaintiffs allowed to recover the 50m rupiah spent on an Indonesian law firm?
answer: The court found it sufficiently clear that the plaintiffs engaged the Indonesian Firm pursuant to Cheo's advice, so they were entitled to claim the 50m rupiah they incurred.
evidence_quote: the plaintiffs' act of engaging the Indonesian Firm is pursuant to Cheo's advice; hence the plaintiffs are entitled to claim the 50m rupiah which they incurred in this respect.

question: If a taxi driver causes a road accident, does the court hold them to a higher expectation because they drive for a living?
answer: In one case the court said professional drivers such as taxi drivers should lead the way in safe and courteous driving and be role models for other drivers, and found the accident was caused solely by the taxi driver's negligence.
evidence_quote: I think that it is not requiring much for professional drivers such as the defendant to lead the way in safe and courteous driving.

question: In Cheng William v Allister Lim & Thrumurgan [2015] SGCA 15, in what proportions were the third parties ordered to contribute to the plaintiffs' costs of the main action?
answer: The Court of Appeal ordered the third parties to contribute in proportion to the apportioned liability: Cheng to contribute 65% and Ng 5% of the plaintiffs' costs for which the defendants were liable.
evidence_quote: Hence, Cheng should contribute towards 65% of the Plaintiffs' costs for which the Defendants are liable and Ng should contribute towards 5% of such costs.

question: In Cheo Yeoh & Associates LLC v AEL [2015] SGCA 29, could the court find facts in favour of respondents who did not themselves testify?
answer: Yes. The Court of Appeal held nothing prevented the court from making a finding of fact based on another respondent's evidence and accepting it in favour of the Absent Respondents, and it dismissed the appeal with costs.
evidence_quote: there was nothing to prevent the court from making a finding of fact on the basis of another Respondent's evidence and accepting it in favour of the Absent Respondents

question: In Cheo Yeoh & Associates LLC v AEL [2015] SGCA 29, what did the solicitors argue about whom Cheo owed a duty of care to?
answer: They argued Cheo was engaged only to help draft the New Will, so he owed a duty only to the Testator and not to the beneficiaries, who were third parties with no proximity under the Spandeck framework, and that policy considerations also militated against a duty.
evidence_quote: Cheo only owed a duty of care to the Testator and not the beneficiaries of the New Will since the latter were third parties to the solicitor-client relationship

question: In Chua Ser Kenon v Karuppiah Jai Sankar [2015] SGHC 127, what did the court decide about the award for the plaintiff's hip injury and his claim for loss of earning capacity?
answer: The court upheld the AR's nominal award of $1,000 and agreed the alternative claim for loss of earning capacity failed, as there was no evidence he would lose his job.
evidence_quote: Consequently, I am of the view that the learned AR's award of $1,000 as a nominal sum is correct.

question: Can I claim for loss of earning capacity after an injury if there's no sign I'll actually lose my job?
answer: Such a claim may fail. In one case the claim was rightly dismissed because there was no evidence the injured plaintiff would lose his job; the evidence suggested he would eventually improve his position.
evidence_quote: There is no evidence that the plaintiff would lose his job. The evidence is to the contrary — that he would eventually improve his position.

question: In Sports Connection Pte Ltd v Asia Law Corp [2015] SGHC 213, what became of the Law Society complaint against Mr Shahiran, and what was the outcome of the action against ALC and SSLC?
answer: The complaint alleging gross overcharging was dismissed by the Law Society in November 2011, and Sports Connection's action against ALC and SSLC was dismissed in its entirety with costs.
evidence_quote: The Law Society Complaint was dismissed by the Law Society in November 2011.

question: In Goel Adesh Kumar v Resorts World at Sentosa [2015] SGHC 289, what were the total damages awarded and what amount was the Casino liable for?
answer: The total damages awarded were $45,915.74, made up of items including $4,000 for false imprisonment and $25,000 for the shoulder injuries, and the Casino was liable for 80% of that total, namely $36,732.59.
evidence_quote: The Casino is liable for $36,732.59, that being 80% of the total damages that I have awarded ( ie , $45,915.74).

question: Is suing the school for negligence the only legal answer to bullying?
answer: No. One court observed that controlling bullying in schools and elsewhere is not simply a matter for the tort of negligence and requires a broader response by society and Parliament.
evidence_quote: the control of bullying in schools and elsewhere is not simply a matter for the tort of negligence. It requires a broader response by society and Parliament.

question: When a court decides whether someone owed me a duty of care, can that duty be defined in very broad terms?
answer: Usually not. The scope of a duty of care should be defined with reference to the injury or loss claimed; it is wrong to frame it as a duty to act in a specific way, but often also inappropriate to frame it in excessively broad terms.
evidence_quote: while it is wrong to frame the duty of care owed as a duty to act in a specific way, it is often also inappropriate to frame the duty of care in excessively broad terms.

question: In Nava Bharat (Singapore) Pte Ltd v Straits Law Practice LLC [2016] SGCA 12, why did the Court of Appeal find that the alleged breach regarding the oral undertaking had diminished causative force?
answer: The court was satisfied the plaintiff agreed to make the loan and release US$3m because it considered it had adequate security in the share pledge agreement, so it dismissed the appeal.
evidence_quote: the plaintiff agreed to make the loan and to release the sum of US$3m because it considered that it had adequate security for that loan in the share pledge agreement.

question: In The Estate of Lee Rui Feng Dominique Sarron v Najib Hanuk Bin Muhammad Jalal [2016] SGHC 119, what costs were awarded to the defendants and the Attorney-General?
answer: The court found the costs sought reasonable and awarded costs inclusive of disbursements of $6,000 each to D1 and D2 and $10,000 to the AG.
evidence_quote: I therefore awarded costs of the respective applications and the action (inclusive of disbursements) to D1 and D2 ($6,000 each) and the AG ($10,000).

question: In Tan Bee Hock v F G Builders Pte Ltd [2016] SGHC 37, what did the court find caused the plaintiff's accident?
answer: The court found the accident resulted from the plaintiff proceeding with haste over the Left Plate without regard to the presence of the Plates, and dismissed the claim with costs.
evidence_quote: the accident was a result of the Plaintiff's conduct in proceeding with haste over the Left Plate and without regard to presence of the Plates.

question: If I get hurt at a worksite and sue the contractor, who has to prove that the contractor's failures caused my injury?
answer: The injured claimant bears the burden of showing that the defendant's acts and omissions breached a duty of care or statutory duty and that those breaches caused the injuries and damage.
evidence_quote: the burden is on the Plaintiff to show that the Defendant's acts and omissions were a breach of a duty of care or statutory duty and that these breaches caused the Plaintiff's injuries and damage.

question: If a company breaks a safety law and I get hurt, can I automatically sue them just for breaking that law?
answer: Not automatically. A claim for breach of statutory duty requires a private right of civil action, meaning you are in a class Parliament intended to protect, and you must also show the breach caused your damage and the damage is within the statute's scope of protection.
evidence_quote: The Plaintiff may sue the Defendant for breach of statutory duty only in circumstances where he has a private right of civil action against the Defendant for the breach of a statutory duty in the first place.

question: In Tan Bee Hock v F G Builders Pte Ltd [2016] SGHC 37, what three elements must a plaintiff show to succeed in the tort of negligence?
answer: Citing Spandeck, the court said the plaintiff must show that the defendant owed a duty of care, breached that duty, and that the breach caused the plaintiff damage.
evidence_quote: the Plaintiff must show that (a) the Defendant owed the Plaintiff a duty of care; (b) the Defendant breached this duty of care; and, (c) the Defendant's breach caused the Plaintiff damage.

question: In Wibowo Boediono v Cristian Priwisata Yacob [2018] SGCA 38, what did the Court of Appeal do with the Judge's order at [343] of the trial judgment?
answer: It set aside the Judge's order at [343] to the extent that it pertained to Mdm Koh's liability, and directed costs submissions limited to 15 pages each within 14 days.
evidence_quote: We set aside the Judge's order at [343] of the Judgment to the extent that it pertains to Mdm Koh's liability.

question: In Ten Leu Jiun Jeanne-marie v National University of Singapore [2018] SGHC 158, what hope did the court express at the end of its judgment?
answer: Although attempts to resolve or mediate the dispute had failed, the court hoped the parties would reach a compromise that would see the plaintiff finally awarded the Degree.
evidence_quote: it is still this court's hope that the parties will somehow reach a compromise which will see the Plaintiff being awarded the Degree finally.

question: In Zhang Run Zi v Ascentsia Law Corporation [2018] SGHC 183, what costs order did the court make when dismissing the claim?
answer: The court dismissed Zhang's claim with costs fixed at $200,000 in the aggregate payable to the Defendants, plus disbursements of $5,836.63.
evidence_quote: I therefore dismissed her claim with costs fixed at $200,000 in the aggregate to be paid to the Defendants, with disbursements at $5,836.63.

question: In JWR Pte Ltd v Edmond Pereira Law Corporation [2019] SGHC 266, why did the court decline to impose a costs sanction on the plaintiff despite weaknesses in its case?
answer: Although parts of the plaintiff's case were not well founded or supported by evidence, the trial was relatively brief, so no sanction was necessary; the claim was dismissed.
evidence_quote: given the relative brevity of the trial, it was not necessary for any sanction to be imposed on the plaintiff.

question: In Anil Singh Gurm v J.S. Yeh & Co [2020] SGHC 151, at what amount were the defendants' pre-trial costs allowed?
answer: The court allowed the defendants' pre-trial costs at $60,000, noting the trial took five days and raised no novel or complex legal issues though the matter took over four years.
evidence_quote: I was thus of the view that the defendants' pre-trial costs would reasonably and fairly be allowed at $60,000

question: When I hire a lawyer to handle my property purchase, what standard of care is the lawyer expected to meet?
answer: In one case the conveyancing solicitors accepted that they owed a duty to exercise reasonable care and skill, and that the applicable standard was that of a reasonably competent conveyancing lawyer.
evidence_quote: They also concurred that the applicable standard of care in the present case was that of a "reasonably competent conveyancing lawyer".

question: If I turn down a settlement offer and then do worse at trial, could I end up paying more of the other side's legal costs?
answer: Yes. In one case where the plaintiff failed to beat an offer to settle, costs were awarded to the defendants on the standard basis up to service of the offer and on the higher indemnity basis thereafter.
evidence_quote: costs be awarded to the defendants on the standard basis up to the service of the offer to settle and thereafter on an indemnity basis

question: In Kevin Bennett Gomez v Bird & Bird ATMD LLP [2022] SGHC(A) 42, what costs did the Appellate Division award on dismissing the appeal?
answer: The court dismissed the appeal and awarded the respondents costs of the appeal and SUM 5 fixed at $70,000 all-in.
evidence_quote: we award the respondents costs of the appeal and SUM 5 fixed at $70,000 (all-in).

question: In Serene Tiong Sze Yin v Chan Herng Nieng [2022] SGHC 170, what unusual relationship framed the court's application of duty-of-care principles?
answer: The case involved the duty of care owed by a doctor, a psychiatrist, to his patient who was simultaneously his paramour.
evidence_quote: the duty of care owed by a doctor to his patient who is simultaneously his paramour.

question: In Serene Tiong Sze Yin v Chan Herng Nieng [2022] SGHC 170, who succeeded and who was ordered to pay costs?
answer: The court ruled against Ms Tiong and ordered her to pay Dr Chan's costs, to be agreed or taxed, while noting Dr Chan would bear the shame of his conduct being aired publicly.
evidence_quote: Ms Tiong is to pay costs, to be agreed or taxed, to Dr Chan.

question: In CXN v CXO [2022] SGHC 311, how was liability for the plaintiff's injuries apportioned between the two defendants?
answer: The court apportioned liability 65% to the first defendant and 35% to the second defendant, granting interlocutory judgment for the plaintiff at 100% with damages to be assessed.
evidence_quote: (a) the first defendant: 65%; and (b) the second defendant: 35%.

question: In Lawrence Li See Kit v Debate Association (Singapore) [2023] SGHC 154, why did the claim for damages in tort fail?
answer: The plaintiff had not shown on the balance of probabilities that the Deceased suffered from an ASR and that this caused him to end his own life.
evidence_quote: it has not been shown on the balance of probabilities that the Deceased suffered from an ASR and consequently that this had caused him to end his own life.

question: Once my lawyer has finished the work and sent the bill, do they still have a duty to keep advising me on that matter?
answer: Generally not without clear evidence. In one case the court held the law firm's duty to draft and advise ended when its invoice was rendered, as there was no clear and explicit evidence that the clients' reliance continued after the job was done.
evidence_quote: There must be clear and explicit evidence that the Lenders' reliance on CNP for this legal issue continues after the job has been done, but there is none.

question: In The Enterprise Fund III Ltd v CNPLaw LLP [2023] SGHC 345, on what date did the court find CNP's duty to provide further drafting and advice ended?
answer: The court found CNP's duty ended on 3 August 2015, when the invoice was rendered to the Lenders, and dismissed the negligence claim.
evidence_quote: CNP's duty to provide further drafting and advice ended on 3 August 2015 when the invoice was rendered to the Lenders.

question: In Cheng Hoe Soon v Ezekiel Peter Latimer [2023] SGHC 53, who acknowledged they would bear the costs of the appeal?
answer: The plaintiff's past and present solicitors acknowledged they would bear all costs, including the costs of the appeal, so referral of the errant solicitors to the Law Society may not be necessary; the appeal was allowed.
evidence_quote: the past and present solicitors for the Plaintiff will bear all costs including the costs of this appeal.

question: In Crapper Ian Anthony v Salmizan Bin Abdullah [2024] SGCA 21, must causation and damage be admitted before parties can enter a consent interlocutory judgment?
answer: No. Although causation and damage are necessary elements of liability in negligence, the Court of Appeal held it does not follow that they must be admitted for parties to enter a consent interlocutory judgment, and allowed the appeal.
evidence_quote: it does not follow that causation and damage must necessarily be admitted for parties to enter into a consent interlocutory judgment.

question: In Cix v Dgn [2024] SGHC 133, what costs order was made against the Seller in favour of Phoenix?
answer: The court ordered the Seller to pay indemnity costs to Phoenix.
evidence_quote: I thus order the Seller to pay indemnity costs to Phoenix.

question: In Lim Chun Yong v Jeffrey Yap [2024] SGHC 150, what total sum was the plaintiff granted judgment for?
answer: The plaintiff was granted judgment in the total sum of $4,700,960.28.
evidence_quote: I grant the plaintiff judgment in the total sum of $4,700,960.28

question: When can a business be held responsible for an accident caused by someone working for it?
answer: Courts apply a two-stage test: the relationship between the wrongdoer and the defendant must be close enough to make it fair, just and reasonable to impose liability, and there must be a sufficient connection between that relationship and the commission of the wrong.
evidence_quote: the relationship between the primary tortfeasor and defendant must be a relationship of sufficient closeness such as would make it fair, just and reasonable to impose liability on the defendant

question: In Lim Chun Yong v Jeffrey Yap [2024] SGHC 150, what factors did the court say must be considered in determining each tortfeasor's contribution?
answer: Following Cheng William, both causative responsibility and blameworthiness must be considered, with blameworthiness being a broad concept that allows a wide range of conduct to be taken into account.
evidence_quote: in "determining each party's contribution, both causative responsibility and blameworthiness have to be considered".

question: In Robert Tantular v the Stephanie Karina [2025] SGHC(A) 8, what costs were fixed after the appeal was dismissed, and why were they moderated?
answer: Costs were fixed at S$45,000 all-in because, although the Appellant failed, the court had rejected the Respondent's submissions on several issues, such as whether THY was an ad hoc fiduciary.
evidence_quote: In the circumstances, we fix costs in the amount of S$45,000 (all-in).

question: In Robert Tantular v the Stephanie Karina [2025] SGHC(A) 8, what test did the Appellate Division state for the existence of a duty of care?
answer: The test is the two-stage test of proximity and policy considerations, preceded by a preliminary requirement of factual foreseeability, as set out in Spandeck.
evidence_quote: the relevant test in relation to a duty of care is the two-stage test premised on proximity and policy considerations, preceded by a preliminary requirement of factual foreseeability

question: If the documents my lawyer relied on were notarised, does that automatically mean my lawyer took enough care?
answer: No. The presumption of regularity for notarised documents is a rule about admitting documents and cannot apply directly to a solicitor's duty of care; whether the solicitor met the standard of a reasonably competent solicitor depends on all the circumstances.
evidence_quote: whether solicitors meet their standard of care even though they make use of notarised documents would depend on all the circumstances.

question: If my lawyer loses my case, does that automatically mean they were negligent?
answer: No. The required standard is that of a reasonably competent and diligent solicitor, not a guarantee of success.
evidence_quote: The requisite standard of care is that of a reasonably competent and diligent solicitor and not one of a guarantee of success

question: What do I have to show to sue a public body for deliberately abusing its powers against me?
answer: In one case a text was cited for the proposition that misfeasance in public office requires an act by a public officer or body done maliciously or knowing it is ultra vires, where damage to the plaintiff is foreseeable and actually caused.
evidence_quote: (a) the act is done maliciously or with the knowledge that it is ultra vires the power of the public body; (b) it is foreseeable that the act would cause damage to the plaintiffs;

question: I paid someone to convert and send my money overseas and they used an unlicensed remittance company without telling me. Did they fall short of their duty?
answer: In one case the court held that, absent any discussion with the client about using a licensed remittance company, it was incumbent on the person to inform the client if he planned to use an unlicensed one; failing to do so fell far short of his standard of care.
evidence_quote: it would then be incumbent on him to inform her if he planned to use an unlicensed one. Joseph did none of these of things, and fell far short of his standard of care.

question: What do I need to prove to win a negligence claim after a road accident?
answer: You must establish a duty of care, breach of that duty, a causal connection between the breach and your damage, and that the damage was not so unforeseeable as to be too remote.
evidence_quote: (a) the existence of a duty of care; (b) breach of the duty of care; (c) a causal connection between the breach and the plaintiff's damage; and (d) the plaintiff's damage was not so unforeseeable as to be too remote.

question: If a consultant writes a report knowing both the buyer and the seller in a deal will rely on it, can the seller hold the consultant responsible for careless mistakes?
answer: Potentially yes. In one case the court found it foreseeable that both buyer and seller might suffer loss from a negligently prepared report they were known to rely on, and that there was sufficient proximity for a prima facie duty of care.
evidence_quote: there is also sufficient proximity for a prima facie duty of care.

question: If a lawyer acting for someone else carelessly carries out that client's instructions and it harms me, what duty does the lawyer owe me?
answer: The solicitor's duty to the third party is to take reasonable care in performing the original undertakings to the client, which is the same duty of care the solicitor owes the client.
evidence_quote: duty to the third party in these situations is to take reasonable care in performing his original undertakings to the client.

question: If I insist on recovering a debt only by bankrupting the debtor and ignore other ways of getting paid, can that weaken my negligence claim against my lawyer?
answer: Yes. In one case it was found that, even if causation were established, the claimant failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate his losses because he insisted on full satisfaction through bankrupting the debtor instead of exploring an alternative recovery route.
evidence_quote: the appellant had failed to take reasonable steps to mitigate his losses as he was insistent that full satisfaction of the Judgment Sum had to come from bankrupting Mr Kuhadas

question: If I signed documents without checking what was in them and was then defrauded, am I automatically treated as partly to blame for my loss?
answer: Not automatically. In one case the trial judge rejected the submission that the victims were contributorily negligent for signing documents without checking their contents, and found they took reasonable steps to mitigate by doing a STARS search and filing a caveat.
evidence_quote: the Judge rejected the submission that the Yacobs were contributorily negligent for signing documents without checking their contents

question: After the other driver agrees they're liable for an accident, can they still argue at the damages stage that I was partly at fault?
answer: According to the approach described from Clarke LJ, at the assessment of damages stage a defendant may not take any point inconsistent with the liability alleged in the statement of claim, including contributory negligence, failure to mitigate, causation and quantum.
evidence_quote: at the AD Stage, the defendant may not take any point inconsistent with the liability alleged in the statement of claim. Such points would include contributory negligence, failure to mitigate, causation, and quantum.

question: If I promise to do something I'm already legally required to do in return for someone else's promise, is that enough to make the deal binding?
answer: Generally not. Where a party is already under a statutory or other legal obligation to do what they undertake, courts will generally not accept that undertaking as good consideration.
evidence_quote: Where the claimant is already under a statutory or other legal obligation to do what he undertakes to the defendant to do in return for the defendant's promise, the courts will generally not accept that his undertaking constitutes good consideration.

question: Can I sue my former lawyers on the basis that their poor advice cost me the chance of winning more money in an earlier lawsuit?
answer: Such claims can be framed as the loss of a chance to recover substantial damages, but the lawyers may dispute the scope of their duty, breach and causation and allege failure to mitigate and contributory negligence, and the court noted it is hardly straightforward to prove such a case.
evidence_quote: Sports Connection's contention is that, owing to the defendants' negligence, it lost the chance of recovering substantial damages in Suit 630.

question: What does someone have to prove to show they were wrongly confined by security staff?
answer: False imprisonment protects against loss of liberty without lawful authority; it is made out if the defendant directly and intentionally causes the plaintiff to be confined within an area delimited by the defendant without a lawful basis.
evidence_quote: The tort is made out if the defendant directly and intentionally causes the plaintiff to be confined within a particular area delimited by the defendant without a lawful basis.

question: Is following road safety habits just a matter of good manners, or can it have legal consequences?
answer: One court stressed that road etiquette is not mere social etiquette, because proper observance of safety precautions can make the difference between safety and injury.
evidence_quote: Times and practices have changed, but road etiquette is not mere social etiquette. Proper observance of safety precautions can be a difference between safety and injury

question: If a doctor who is also my partner gives me prescription pills freely and I become addicted, what kind of claim might I bring?
answer: In one case the claimant alleged medical negligence, arguing the doctor, as her de facto doctor, owed a duty to ensure she would not become addicted and breached it by giving Xanax without checking its suitability or guarding against addiction.
evidence_quote: Dr Chan breached his duty of care when he freely gave Xanax to Ms Tiong without (a) ascertaining the suitability of Xanax for her; and (b) ensuring that she would not become addicted to Xanax.

question: Can a person who prays over someone in a religious setting be held to owe a duty not to cause them psychological harm?
answer: In one case the defendants argued policy against such a duty: Singapore values racial and religious harmony, imposing it on faith leaders would cause a flood of claims, and they would avoid giving spiritual assistance.
evidence_quote: To impose a duty of care on priests, pastors, mediums, imams or any person of the faith not to cause psychiatric harm to people who request prayer will lead to a flood of claims and complaints.

question: In AEL v Cheo Yeoh & Associates LLC [2014] SGHC 129, how did the court treat the threshold of factual foreseeability for the solicitor's duty to will beneficiaries?
answer: The court held the threshold of factual foreseeability was easily overcome, because Cheo was engaged for the proper drafting and execution of the New Will, the instrument by which the Testator bequeathed his assets.
evidence_quote: In my view, the threshold of factual foreseeability is easily overcome in the present case. Cheo is engaged for the proper drafting and execution of the New Will.

question: In Ayw v Ayx [2015] SGHC 312, on what basis did the court decide the plaintiff's bullying claim against the school at the striking-out stage?
answer: Having considered the pleaded case and the parties' submissions, the court struck out the plaintiff's entire claim, despite the novel questions about a school's duty regarding bullying and aggravated damages in negligence.
evidence_quote: I am striking out the plaintiff's entire claim on the ground

question: In CXN v CXO [2022] SGHC 311, where was the 8-year-old plaintiff seated when the collision occurred?
answer: The plaintiff was in the van's rear cargo compartment, which had neither seats nor seat belts, and was ejected from the van in the collision.
evidence_quote: The plaintiff, who was then 8 years of age, was on board the van in the rear cargo compartment, which had neither seats nor seat belts.

question: In Lyu Yan @ Lu Yan v Lim Tien Chiang [2020] SGHC 145, what defence did all the defendants raise concerning the Agreement?
answer: They argued the Agreement was illegal under Chinese law and therefore void and unenforceable in Singapore as contrary to public policy.
evidence_quote: The defendants all raised the defence that the Agreement is illegal under Chinese law, and therefore void and unenforceable in Singapore as being contrary to public policy.

question: In Kevin Bennett Gomez v Bird & Bird ATMD LLP [2022] SGHC(A) 42, why did the element of causation fail?
answer: The evidence indicated that Mr Kuhadas did not have the funds or means to satisfy the entire Judgment Sum, so causation was not proven by the appellant.
evidence_quote: The element of causation was therefore not proven by the appellant

question: In Cheng William v Allister Lim & Thrumurgan [2015] SGCA 15, what was the first aspect of the trial judge's decision with which the Court of Appeal disagreed?
answer: The Court of Appeal held the Judge should have made a finding of contributory negligence on Su's part, having regard to the evidence, the facts found and the pleadings.
evidence_quote: the Judge made no finding of contributory negligence on Su's part. In our judgment, such a finding should have been made having regard to the evidence, the facts that were found, and the pleadings.

question: Can a civil claim still be brought for the common law tort of harassment in Singapore, and how did the court in Ayw v Ayx [2015] SGHC 312 treat the Protection from Harassment Act 2014 in that bullying case?
answer: The Protection from Harassment Act 2014 abolished the common law tort of harassment, so no civil proceedings for harassment may be brought except under that Act. In Ayw v Ayx the court noted the Act did not apply to the case before it.
gold_citations: Protection from Harassment Act 2014, s 14(1)|[2015] SGHC 312
evidence_quote: The common law tort of harassment is, to avoid doubt, declared to be abolished and no civil proceedings may be brought for the tort of harassment except under this Act.|The PHA does not of course apply in the present case.

question: What power does the Civil Law Act 1909 give courts to award interest on damages, and at what rate and for what period was interest applied in Lyu Yan @ Lu Yan v Lim Tien Chiang [2020] SGHC 145?
answer: Section 12 lets a court of record include interest at such rate as it thinks fit for any part of the period from when the cause of action arose to judgment. In Lyu Yan the court applied it so interest ran from the date the writ was issued to the date of judgment at 5.33% per annum.
evidence_quote: the court may, if it thinks fit, order that there shall be included in the sum for which judgment is given interest at such rate as it thinks fit|interest on the judgment sum(s) will run from the date on which the writ was issued to the date of this judgment, at 5.33% per annum.

question: In Cheng Hoe Soon v Ezekiel Peter Latimer [2023] SGHC 53, the court described an earlier case in which one claim was time-barred under section 6 of the Limitation Act 1959. What limitation period does section 6 set for contract and tort claims?
answer: The court noted that in Pakirisamy one of the plaintiffs' claims was time-barred under s 6 of the Limitation Act 1959. Section 6(1) provides that actions founded on contract or tort cannot be brought after 6 years from the date the cause of action accrued.
evidence_quote: one of their claims was time-barred under s 6 of the Limitation Act 1959 (2020 Rev Ed)|the following actions shall not be brought after the expiration of 6 years from the date on which the cause of action accrued: (a) actions founded on a contract or on tort;

question: In Cheng William v Allister Lim & Thrumurgan [2015] SGCA 15, the Court of Appeal held a finding of contributory negligence should have been made against Su. Under the Contributory Negligence and Personal Injuries Act 1953, what is the effect of such a finding on damages?
answer: The Court of Appeal held the Judge should have found contributory negligence on Su's part. Under s 3(1), a claim is not defeated by the claimant's own fault, but damages are reduced to the extent the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in responsibility.
gold_citations: [2015] SGCA 15|Contributory Negligence and Personal Injuries Act 1953, s 3(1)
evidence_quote: the Judge made no finding of contributory negligence on Su's part. In our judgment, such a finding should have been made|the damages recoverable in respect thereof shall be reduced to such extent as the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant’s share in the responsibility for the damage.

question: In CXN v CXO [2022] SGHC 311, was the child plaintiff's damages award reduced for his own fault, and what statutory rule governs such reductions?
answer: No reduction applied because neither defendant alleged contributory negligence; interlocutory judgment was entered at 100% and liability apportioned 65% and 35% between the defendants. The Contributory Negligence and Personal Injuries Act 1953 reduces damages only where the claimant's own fault partly caused the damage.
gold_citations: [2022] SGHC 311|Contributory Negligence and Personal Injuries Act 1953, s 3(1)
evidence_quote: Neither of the defendants allege contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff.|Where any person suffers damage as the result partly of his own fault and partly of the fault of any other person or persons

question: In Chew Kim Kee v Kertar and Co [2004] SGHC 95, the solicitors did not file a notice of appeal by the deadline. Why did the plaintiff's negligence claim nevertheless fail?
answer: The notice of appeal was due by 5 October 1999 and was not filed, but the court found the plaintiff had in fact acted on the award, exercising the option to buy over the other 65% share of the matrimonial home and later reselling it, so her action was dismissed with costs.
evidence_quote: It is not disputed that the defendant did not file a notice of appeal by 5 October 1999 or at all.|For all those reasons, the plaintiff's action is dismissed with costs.

question: What did the High Court award the will beneficiaries in AEL v Cheo Yeoh & Associates LLC [2014] SGHC 129, and what happened when the solicitors appealed in [2015] SGCA 29?
answer: The High Court held the solicitors negligent and awarded the plaintiffs their total claimed loss of AUD$719,375.36 and 50m rupiah. The Court of Appeal dismissed the solicitors' appeal with costs.
evidence_quote: entitled to their total claimed loss of AUD$719,375.36 and 50m rupiah.|In the result, we dismiss the Appellants' appeal with costs and the usual consequential orders.

question: How did Kevin Bennett Gomez's negligence claim against Bird & Bird ATMD LLP fare at first instance in [2021] SGHC 230 and on appeal in [2022] SGHC(A) 42, and what costs were ordered?
answer: The High Court dismissed Suit 198 and, because he failed to beat an offer to settle, awarded the defendants costs on the standard basis up to the offer and indemnity basis after. The Appellate Division dismissed his appeal and fixed costs of the appeal and SUM 5 at $70,000 all-in.
evidence_quote: I therefore dismissed Suit 198 as against both the defendants.|For the foregoing reasons, we dismiss the appeal.

question: In the Salmizan Bin Abdullah v Crapper Ian Anthony litigation, what costs order did the High Court make in [2023] SGHC 75, and what was the outcome of the appeal in [2024] SGCA 21?
answer: The High Court made no order as to costs because the application was taken out jointly by both parties. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, answering Question 1 in the affirmative.
evidence_quote: Since this application was taken out jointly by both the plaintiff and the defendant, I make no order as to costs.|For the above reasons, we allowed the appeal.

question: In Goel Adesh Kumar v Resorts World at Sentosa [2015] SGHC 289, what must be shown for the tort of false imprisonment, and how much was awarded for it?
answer: False imprisonment is made out where the defendant directly and intentionally causes the plaintiff to be confined within an area it delimits without lawful basis. The court awarded $4,000 in damages for false imprisonment.
evidence_quote: The tort is made out if the defendant directly and intentionally causes the plaintiff to be confined within a particular area delimited by the defendant without a lawful basis.|(a) damages for false imprisonment: $4,000;

question: Which Court of Appeal decision did the High Court in Lim Chun Yong v Jeffrey Yap [2024] SGHC 150 rely on for assessing contribution between tortfeasors, and how was contribution to costs apportioned in that Court of Appeal case?
answer: It relied on Cheng William v Allister Lim & Thrumurgan, which requires considering both causative responsibility and blameworthiness. In Cheng William the Court of Appeal ordered Cheng to contribute 65% and Ng 5% of the plaintiffs' costs for which the defendants were liable.
evidence_quote: As the Court of Appeal held at [45] of Cheng William , in "determining each party's contribution, both causative responsibility and blameworthiness have to be considered".|Hence, Cheng should contribute towards 65% of the Plaintiffs' costs for which the Defendants are liable and Ng should contribute towards 5% of such costs.

question: In Tan Bee Hock v F G Builders Pte Ltd [2016] SGHC 37, what did the plaintiff need to prove in negligence, and why did the claim fail?
answer: The plaintiff had to show a duty of care, breach, and that the breach caused damage. The claim failed because the court found the accident resulted from the plaintiff proceeding hastily over the Left Plate, so he did not discharge his burden.
evidence_quote: the Plaintiff must show that (a) the Defendant owed the Plaintiff a duty of care; (b) the Defendant breached this duty of care; and, (c) the Defendant's breach caused the Plaintiff damage.|the Plaintiff has failed to discharge that burden. For these reasons, I dismiss the Plaintiff's claim with costs to be taxed if not agreed.

question: The High Court in Anwar Patrick Adrian v Ng Chong & Hue LLC [2013] SGHC 202 held the solicitor not liable. How did the High Court in AEL v Cheo Yeoh & Associates LLC [2014] SGHC 129 describe the duty to third parties stated in the Anwar appeal?
answer: In 2013 the High Court dismissed the claim, finding Ng and NC&H not liable. AEL quoted the Anwar appeal judgment as holding that a solicitor's duty to the third party is to take reasonable care in performing the original undertakings to the client, the same duty owed to the client.
evidence_quote: I am of the view that he and NC&H are not liable for the loss claimed by the first and second plaintiffs in this action.|It is, in other words, the same duty of care that the solicitor owed to their client.

question: How did Amutha Valli v Titular Superior of the Redemptorist Fathers [2009] SGHC 35 describe the Spandeck test for a duty of care, and what preliminary requirement did the Appellate Division add in Robert Tantular v the Stephanie Karina [2025] SGHC(A) 8?
answer: Amutha Valli described Spandeck as a two-stage test of proximity and policy considerations. Robert Tantular stated that this two-stage test is preceded by a preliminary requirement of factual foreseeability.
evidence_quote: the test to determine the imposition of a duty of care was a two-staged one of (i) proximity and (ii) policy considerations.|preceded by a preliminary requirement of factual foreseeability

question: Under the Evidence Act 1893, who bears the burden of proving facts on which a claim depends, and how did that play out in Tan Bee Hock v F G Builders Pte Ltd [2016] SGHC 37?
answer: Whoever asks the court for judgment on a right or liability that depends on facts they assert must prove those facts. In Tan Bee Hock the plaintiff bore the burden to show breach and causation, failed to discharge it, and his claim was dismissed.
evidence_quote: Whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability, dependent on the existence of facts which the person asserts, must prove that those facts exist.|the burden is on the Plaintiff to show that the Defendant's acts and omissions were a breach of a duty of care or statutory duty

question: The Penal Code 1871 provides that theft is punishable with imprisonment of up to 3 years. Under the Interpretation Act 1965, must a court impose the full 3 years?
answer: No. Theft is punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both, and the Interpretation Act provides that a penalty prescribed for an offence is a maximum, so the offence is punishable by a penalty not exceeding that provided.
evidence_quote: Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 3 years, or with fine, or with both.|such provision implies that the offence shall be punishable upon conviction by a penalty not exceeding (except as may be otherwise expressly mentioned in the written law) the penalty provided.

question: After an accused is convicted, what must the court hear before sentencing under the Criminal Procedure Code 2010, and what alternative to sentencing does the Probation of Offenders Act 1951 allow?
answer: The court must hear any plea in mitigation by the accused, with the prosecution having a right of reply. Instead of sentencing, the court may make a probation order placing the offender under supervision for between 6 months and 3 years, if the sentence is not fixed by law.
gold_citations: Criminal Procedure Code 2010, s 228(3)|Probation of Offenders Act 1951, s 5(1)
evidence_quote: The court must then hear any plea in mitigation of sentence by the accused and the prosecution has a right of reply.|the court may, instead of sentencing him, make a probation order

question: How do the Misuse of Drugs Act 1973 and the Intoxicating Substances Act 1987 each treat self-consumption: consuming a controlled drug versus inhaling an intoxicating substance?
answer: Under the Misuse of Drugs Act it is an offence, unless authorised, to smoke, administer to oneself or otherwise consume a controlled drug. Under the Intoxicating Substances Act it is an offence to use or inhale an intoxicating substance to induce intoxication in oneself.
gold_citations: Misuse of Drugs Act 1973, s 8(b)|Intoxicating Substances Act 1987, s 3(1)
evidence_quote: smoke, administer to himself or herself or otherwise consume|A person must not, for the purpose of inducing or causing in himself or herself a state of intoxication, use or inhale any intoxicating substance.

question: In Zhang Run Zi v Ascentsia Law Corporation [2018] SGHC 183, the claim against the law firm was commenced shortly before it became time-barred. What general limitation period applies to contract and tort actions under the Limitation Act 1959?
answer: Zhang's claim against the law firm was commenced shortly before it became time-barred. Under the Limitation Act 1959, actions founded on contract or tort cannot be brought after 6 years from when the cause of action accrued.
evidence_quote: which was commenced shortly before it became time-barred.|the following actions shall not be brought after the expiration of 6 years from the date on which the cause of action accrued: (a) actions founded on a contract or on tort;

question: Which authority did Tan & Au LLP v Goh Teh Lee [2012] SGHC 130 cite for the standard of care required of solicitors, and how did JWR Pte Ltd v Edmond Pereira Law Corporation [2019] SGHC 266 state that standard?
answer: Tan & Au cited Zhou Tong v Public Prosecutor, where V K Rajah JA reiterated the standard of care and skill required of solicitors. JWR stated the standard is that of a reasonably competent and diligent solicitor, not a guarantee of success.
evidence_quote: The law relating to the standard of care and skill required of solicitors in the conduct of professional business was reiterated recently in Zhou Tong|The requisite standard of care is that of a reasonably competent and diligent solicitor and not one of a guarantee of success

question: In Lyu Yan @ Lu Yan v Lim Tien Chiang [2020] SGHC 145, how did Joseph breach his standard of care, and what judgment could Lyu Yan elect to take against him?
answer: Joseph fell far short of his standard of care by failing to inform Lyu Yan that he planned to use an unlicensed remittance company. Lyu Yan could elect judgment for US$3m against Joseph, or alternatively RMB sums against Joseph, Jonathan and Derek.
evidence_quote: Joseph did none of these of things, and fell far short of his standard of care.|There will thus be judgment for Lyu Yan, at her election, for either the US$3m against Joseph

question: In Serene Tiong Sze Yin v Chan Herng Nieng [2022] SGHC 170, what was Ms Tiong's primary medical negligence allegation, and who was ordered to pay costs at the end?
answer: Her primary claim was that Dr Chan, as her de facto doctor, breached his duty by freely giving her Xanax without ascertaining its suitability or ensuring she would not become addicted. The court ruled against her and ordered her to pay Dr Chan's costs.
evidence_quote: Ms Tiong's primary claim is that Dr Chan, as her de facto doctor, owed her a duty of care to ensure that she would not be addicted to Xanax.|Ms Tiong is to pay costs, to be agreed or taxed, to Dr Chan.

question: In Sports Connection Pte Ltd v Asia Law Corp [2015] SGHC 213, what loss did Sports Connection claim from its former lawyers' negligence, and what was the outcome against ALC and SSLC?
answer: Sports Connection claimed it lost the chance of recovering substantial damages in Suit 630 because of the defendants' negligence. Its action against ALC and SSLC was dismissed in its entirety with costs.
evidence_quote: it lost the chance of recovering substantial damages in Suit 630.|Sports Connection's action against ALC and SSLC is dismissed in its entirety with costs to be taxed if not agreed.

question: What does the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore require the High Court to do on a complaint of unlawful detention, and does the Prisons Act 1933 limit the High Court's power to have prisoners brought before it?
answer: On a complaint of unlawful detention, the General Division of the High Court must inquire and, unless satisfied the detention is lawful, order the person produced and released. The Prisons Act 1933 expressly does not lessen or affect the court's power to direct confined persons to be brought before it by an Order for Review of Detention.
gold_citations: Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, Art 9(2)|Prisons Act 1933, s 50
evidence_quote: the General Division of the High Court shall inquire into the complaint and, unless satisfied that the detention is lawful|to direct persons confined in Singapore to be brought before the General Division of the High Court by an Order for Review of Detention.

question: Under the Arbitration Act 2001 and the International Arbitration Act 1994, when may a party to an arbitration agreement apply to stay court proceedings brought in breach of it?
answer: Under both Acts a party may apply at any time after filing and serving a notice of intention to contest or not contest and before delivering any pleading or taking any other step; the International Arbitration Act provision applies despite Article 8 of the Model Law.
gold_citations: Arbitration Act 2001, s 6(1)|International Arbitration Act 1994, s 6(1)
evidence_quote: may, at any time after filing and serving a notice of intention to contest or not contest and before delivering any pleading|Despite Article 8 of the Model Law, where any party to an arbitration agreement to which this Act applies institutes any proceedings in any court

question: How does the Penal Code 1871 define criminal defamation, and what can a person who innocently published defamatory words do under the Defamation Act 1957 to avoid libel proceedings?
answer: Criminal defamation involves making or publishing an imputation about a person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe it will harm, their reputation. Under the Defamation Act, an innocent publisher may make an offer of amends, which if accepted and performed bars libel or slander proceedings by that party.
evidence_quote: makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person, intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person|if the offer is accepted by the party aggrieved and is duly performed, no proceedings for libel or slander shall be taken or continued by that party

question: If a person dies partly through their own fault and partly through someone else's negligence, can dependants still sue under the Civil Law Act 1909, and how are their damages affected under the Contributory Negligence and Personal Injuries Act 1953?
answer: Yes. The wrongdoer remains liable to an action for damages for the benefit of the dependants despite the death. But where the deceased was partly at fault, damages recoverable by dependants under section 20 of the Civil Law Act are reduced to a proportionate extent.
gold_citations: Civil Law Act 1909, s 20(1)|Contributory Negligence and Personal Injuries Act 1953, s 3(5)
evidence_quote: the person who would have been liable if death had not ensued shall be liable to an action for damages, notwithstanding the death of the person injured.|any damages recoverable in an action brought for the benefit of — (a) the dependants of that person under section 20 of the Civil Law Act 1909;

question: How does the punishment for detaining someone to compel the Government to act under the Hostage-Taking Act 2010 compare with the punishment for kidnapping for ransom under the Kidnapping Act 1961?
answer: Both carry death or imprisonment for life. Hostage-taking to compel the Government, a foreign government or an international intergovernmental organisation is punishable with death or life imprisonment plus liability to fine or caning; kidnapping for ransom is punishable with death or life imprisonment plus liability to caning.
evidence_quote: the Government, the government of another State or an international intergovernmental organisation to do or abstain from doing any act shall be guilty of an offence, and shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life|shall be guilty of an offence and shall be punished on conviction with death or imprisonment for life and shall, if he is not sentenced to death, also be liable to caning.

question: In Lim Chun Yong v Jeffrey Yap [2024] SGHC 150, what did the sixth defendant argue about the burden of proof and res ipsa loquitur, and what was the plaintiff ultimately awarded?
answer: The sixth defendant argued the plaintiff bore the burden of proving negligence against each defendant and that res ipsa loquitur could not apply. The court ultimately granted the plaintiff judgment totalling $4,700,960.28.
evidence_quote: the sixth defendant argues that the burden is on the plaintiff to prove his claim for negligence against each of the defendants, and the res ipsa loquitur doctrine cannot be applied.|I grant the plaintiff judgment in the total sum of $4,700,960.28

question: What must a person have to practise as an advocate and solicitor under the Legal Profession Act 1966, and what standard of care did Chew Kim Kee v Kertar and Co [2004] SGHC 95 say such a practitioner must meet?
answer: The person's name must be on the roll and they must hold a practising certificate in force. Chew Kim Kee recognised the obligation to exercise the care and skill of a competent practitioner, breached if they omit to do what a reasonably competent advocate and solicitor would have done.
gold_citations: Legal Profession Act 1966, s 32(1)|[2004] SGHC 95 at [11]–[14]
evidence_quote: (b) he or she has in force a practising certificate.|one of the obligations of an advocate and solicitor in carrying out his retainer is to exercise the care and skill of a competent practitioner in the discharge of his duties
